# Adventure and quest lens

Apply to adventure, journey, survival, heist, and quest narratives. Focus on objective, obstacles, decisions, changing stakes, and consequences; do not reduce every journey to a fixed "hero's journey" pattern.

## Chapter-level prompts

- Track the immediate and overarching objective, who owns it, why it matters, constraints, and what would count as success or failure.
- Record obstacles and their source (environmental, social, antagonist, internal, resource-based); explain how the protagonist responds and what the response costs.
- Follow changes to resources, knowledge, alliances, route, time pressure, and risk. Note practical continuity only when relevant to causality.
- Identify a turning point in which a choice, setback, discovery, or reversal changes the plan or stakes.
- For survival narratives, track credible needs and constraints (shelter, food, injury, weather, fatigue) only as supported by the text; do not fill in technical facts without research.
- For heists, follow objective, team roles, plan assumptions, contingencies, execution, and deviations, preserving reveals according to chapter order.

## Whole-work prompts

- Map the causal chain from goal through escalating obstacles to climax and outcome; distinguish detours that change the protagonist from those that only delay progress.
- Assess whether victories and failures follow from established skills, choices, resources, and constraints.
- Trace shifts in the meaning of the destination, treasure, mission, or return; note how relationships and values change through the journey.

## Guardrails

- Do not impose a monomyth or fixed beat sheet as the only valid structure.
- Avoid converting unsupported geography, survival, or technical details into fact.
- Keep chapter analyses limited to information available by that point.
